front_blocks.md: Define **activity**.

back_blocks.md: The **rate** at which unstable nuclei in a radioactive source **decay**, measured in **becquerels (Bq)**.

front_blocks.md: Define the **becquerel**.

back_blocks.md: The unit of **activity**; **1 Bq** is equal to **one nucleus decaying per second** in a source.

front_blocks.md: Why does the **activity** of a radioactive source **decrease** over time?

back_blocks.md: Each decay event **reduces the number of radioactive nuclei** remaining in the source, so fewer nuclei are left to decay in each following second.

cards.front_md: Why does the **activity** of a radioactive source **decrease** over time?

front_blocks.md: Which piece of apparatus is used to measure the **count rate** of a radioactive source?

cards.front_md: Which piece of apparatus is used to measure the **count rate** of a radioactive source?

front_blocks.md: What do the **fluctuations** seen when count rate is plotted against time provide evidence for?

back_blocks.md: The **randomness** of radioactive decay.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Activity and count rate mean the same thing.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
**Activity** is the rate at which unstable nuclei **decay**; **count rate** is the rate at which radioactive **emissions are detected** (e.g. by a GM tube).

front_blocks.md: Define **half-life**.

back_blocks.md: The time taken for the **number of nuclei** of a radioactive isotope in a sample to **decrease by half** (equivalently, the time for the sample's activity to fall to half its original value).

cards.front_md: Define **half-life**.
cards.back_md: The time taken for the **number of nuclei** of a radioactive isotope in a sample to **decrease by half** (equivalently, the time for the sample's activity to fall to half its original value).

front_blocks.md: Describe how the half-life of a sample can be determined experimentally.

back_blocks.md: Measure the **initial activity**, *A*~*0*~, of the sample, then measure how the **activity changes with time**. The **half-life** is the time taken for the activity to fall to **half** its original value.

cards.front_md: Describe how the half-life of a sample can be determined experimentally.

front_blocks.md: A sample has an initial activity of 880 Bq. After one year, the activity has fallen to 220 Bq. What is the half-life of this sample?

back_blocks.md: 220 Bq is a **quarter** of 880 Bq, so **two half-lives** have passed in one year. Therefore the half-life of the sample is **6 months**.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
The half-life of a given isotope changes over time.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
The **half-life is constant** for a particular isotope — the time to fall from 100% to 50% activity is the same as the time to fall from 50% to 25%.

front_blocks.md: Define **radiotherapy**.

back_blocks.md: The treatment of cancer using **ionising radiation** (beams of **gamma rays** directed at a tumour), which is different from **chemotherapy** (a drug-based treatment).

cards.front_md: Define **radiotherapy**.

front_blocks.md: Why is **alpha radiation** used in smoke detectors, rather than beta or gamma?

back_blocks.md: Alpha is the **most ionising** and **least penetrating** type of radiation, so it is readily **absorbed by smoke** entering the detector, blocking the ionising current and triggering the alarm. Beta and gamma would mostly pass straight through the smoke without being absorbed.

cards.front_md: Why is **alpha radiation** used in smoke detectors, rather than beta or gamma?
cards.back_md: Alpha is the **most ionising** and **least penetrating** type of radiation, so it is readily **absorbed by smoke** entering the detector, blocking the ionising current and triggering the alarm. Beta and gamma would mostly pass straight through the smoke without being absorbed.

front_blocks.md: Why is **beta radiation**, rather than alpha or gamma, used to monitor the thickness of thin materials such as aluminium foil?

back_blocks.md: Beta radiation is only **partially absorbed**, so the count rate detected changes with thickness. Alpha would be **fully absorbed** regardless of thickness, and gamma would nearly all be **detected** regardless of thickness, so neither can be used to track changes in thickness.

cards.front_md: Why is **beta radiation**, rather than alpha or gamma, used to monitor the thickness of thin materials such as aluminium foil?

front_blocks.md: Why is **gamma radiation** used to sterilise medical equipment?

back_blocks.md: Gamma is the **most penetrating** type of radiation, so it can irradiate **all sides** of the instruments and sterilise them **without removing the packaging**.

cards.front_md: Why is **gamma radiation** used to sterilise medical equipment?

A **thicker** material **absorbs more beta particles**, so the count rate detected **decreases**.

front_blocks.md: Define **contamination** (in radioactivity).

back_blocks.md: The **accidental transfer** of a radioactive substance **onto or into** a material, which causes that material to become **radioactive**.

front_blocks.md: Define **irradiation**.

back_blocks.md: The process of **exposing** a material to **ionising radiation**. Irradiation does **not** make the material radioactive.

front_blocks.md: How can **irradiation** be prevented?

back_blocks.md: By using **shielding**, such as a **lead-lined suit**, which **absorbs** radiation before it reaches the person.

front_blocks.md: How can **contamination** be prevented?

back_blocks.md: By wearing an **airtight suit**, which prevents radioactive atoms getting **onto or into** the person.

front_blocks.md: Why does a source with a **longer half-life** pose a greater **contamination** risk than one with a shorter half-life?

back_blocks.md: A longer half-life means the source **remains radioactive for longer**, so it needs to be controlled, shielded and stored for longer to prevent it spreading.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
An object that has been irradiated becomes radioactive.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
**Irradiation** does not make an object radioactive; only **contamination** (the transfer of radioactive material onto or into it) does.

front_blocks.md: Why are **alpha** sources more dangerous than gamma sources if they get **inside** the body?

back_blocks.md: Alpha is the **most ionising** type of radiation (gamma is around **20 times less ionising**), so alpha causes the **most damage** to living cells when the source is inside the body.

cards.front_md: Why are **alpha** sources more dangerous than gamma sources if they get **inside** the body?
cards.back_md: Alpha is the **most ionising** type of radiation (gamma is around **20 times less ionising**), so alpha causes the **most damage** to living cells when the source is inside the body.

front_blocks.md: Why are **gamma** sources more dangerous than alpha sources if they are **outside** the body?

back_blocks.md: Gamma is the **most penetrating** type of radiation, so it can pass through skin and reach living cells inside the body. Alpha is the **least penetrating** and is absorbed by air before it even reaches the skin.

cards.front_md: Why are **gamma** sources more dangerous than alpha sources if they are **outside** the body?
cards.back_md: Gamma is the **most penetrating** type of radiation, so it can pass through skin and reach living cells inside the body. Alpha is the **least penetrating** and is absorbed by air before it even reaches the skin.

front_blocks.md: Define **dosemeter**.

back_blocks.md: A device (also called a **radiation badge**) that **measures the amount of radiation** a person has been exposed to; it is often worn by radiographers or anyone working with radiation.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Radioactive waste with a long half-life can be safely stored above ground in ordinary containers.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
Long half-life waste stays dangerous for a very long time, so it must be buried **underground** in secure, geologically stable sites, in **strong, corrosion-resistant** containers.

front_blocks.md: What effect can ionising radiation have on the **DNA** within a living cell?

back_blocks.md: It can **damage DNA**. The cell may repair the damage successfully, but an **incorrect repair** can cause a **mutation**, which can lead to **cancer**.
